label: text
text: To-day is Whitmonday and a holiday. Why? According to that greatest of all reference books, the Encyclopaedia Britannica, Whitsunday, "one of the principal feasts of the Christian Church," is celebrated on the fiftieth day after Easter to commemorate the descent of the Holy Spirit on the Disciple. The day became one of the three haptismal seasons, and the name Whitsunday is now generally attributed to the white garments, formerly worn by the candidate.

label: text
text:
for baptism on this feast. The festival is the third in importance of the great feasts of the Church and the last of the annual cycle commemorating the Lord. It is connected with the Jewish Pentecost, not only in the historical date of its origin but in idea, the Jewish festival being one of thanks for the first-fruits of the earth, the Christian for the first-fruits of the Spirit. In the middle ages the Whitsun services were marked by many curious customs. Among these were the letting down of a dove from the roof into the church, the dropping of balls of fire, rose-leaves and the like. Whitsun is one of the Scottish quarter days, and though the Church festival is movable, the legal date was fixed for the 15th day of May by an act of 1693. Whitmonday, which, with the Sunday itself, was the occasion of the greatest of all the medieval church ales, was made an English Bank Holiday by an act passed on the 25th of May, 1871.
So that is why we enjoy a holiday in Hongkong today.

label: text
text: It would be interesting to know what has been the moral effect upon the Chinese in introducing ameliorative measures of reform connected with the labour of children in factories in the Colony. The report for 1924 of the Secretariat for Chinese Affairs in this respect, makes pleasant reading. There was some protest when legislation was urged. It would upset the Chinese; it would interfere with production, wages, household affairs, etc., etc. The result has been nothing of the sort. Three hundred children in factories work in safe and pleasant surroundings, in reasonable hours. The great fact is that a considerable number are prevented from doing so until a reasonable year of discretion has been reached. Incidentally this particular report is an interesting evidence of Chinese industrialism in the Colony. There are 28 factories in Hongkong and Kowloon—a fairly large number of seems—given over to the production of such things as knitting, glass, and fireworks. These factories, but illustrate once again the versatility and ability of the Chinese. label: text
text: One result of the Great War has been the abolition of fixed alliances. These, at one time were a common feature of European and international politics. France and Britain allied; Italy and Germany also; then Japan and Britain. The expiry of the latter treaty and its non-renewal seem definitely to have set the seal on alliances generally. This is all to the good. An alliance of two great powers tended to create suspicion and misunderstanding—and worst of all, jealousy. If anything the League of Nations would have an influence contrary to the creation of alliances. In that body could be discussed questions likely to lead to disruption and war and to find a way to lasting peace. The work of the League can be and is being supplemented, by treaties of a peaceful nature. Thus the latest memorandum of the British Government to France dwells on the necessity of suitable arbitration treaties supplementing the Rhine security pact with a view to guaranteeing the peace of other parts of Europe. Here is further evidence of the "come, let us reason together" policy. At this rate we shall soon be realising that the pen and tongue are mightier than the sword.

label: paragraph_title
text: Deport Them.

label: text
text: Portugal has set an example in the matter of dealing with bomb throwers and insurrectionaries generally. A number of these misguided people have been placed on board a cruiser and are now on their way to Portuguese Guineu—“far, far away.” Hongkong's idea of deportation consists in sending undesirables—principally beggars—to Canton which is not “far, far away.” With steamer fares at cut-throat, competitive prices, a return to the happy hunting ground of the beggar is simplicity itself. Why not fix on some other place to which to send these people? A dumping process of such a nature, faithfully and ceaselessly carried out, would have its own moral effect. Swatow, Amoy, Foochow, might be tried as experiments. Caution the next batch of beggars that a reappearance means exile to other and more distant places than Canton, and some good is likely to accrue. Whilst the nuisance is said to be abating as a result of the efforts recently initiated and maintained, there is a suspicion that when the official back is turned, the beggar, in all his dirt and deformity will be back again.

label: text
text: The Whitsun Whitsun Mysteries were Monday. acted at Chester, seven or eight on each day during the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday in Whitsun week. The drapers, for instance, exhibited the "Creation," the tanners took the "Fall of Lucifer;" the water-carriers of the Dee reproduced the "Deluge;" the cooks had the "Harrowing of Hell." The performers were carried from one station to another by means of a movable scaffold, a huge and ponderous machine mounted on wheels, gaily decorated with flags, and divided into two compartments, the upper of which formed the stage, and the lower, defended from vulgar curiosity by coarse canvas draperies, answered the purposes of the green-room. The performers began at the Abbey gates, where they were witnessed by the high dignitaries of the Church; they then proceeded to the High Cross, where the Mayor and the civic magnates were assembled; and so on, through the city, until their motley history of God and His dealings with man had been played out. The production of these pageants was costly; each mystery has been set down at fifteen or twenty pounds, present money. The dresses were obtained from the churches, until this practice being denounced as scandalous, the guilds had then to provide the costume and other properties.

label: paragraph_title
text: A FALLACY. That Moths Eat Clothes.

label: text
text: This fallacy is somewhat akin to the one that a thaw bursis the water-pipes, for when a thaw comes, then also comes the inconvenience of burst water-pipes. Similarly, when the clothes are taken out and found moth-eaten, and moths fly from them, the too-ready conclusion is that the moths have eaten them. What occurs is this: The clothes' moths lay eggs on suitable materials, these eggs develop into larvae or grubs, which eat the clothes. The larvae then change into pupae, each forming a tiny cocoon (similar to that of a silkworm) for itself, and after some time the cycle of changes is completed by moths emerging from these cocoons, which may be found among clothes that have been badly moth-eaten. So we see that the moths which fly out on the clothes being disturbed are quite innocent of the harm that has been done up to that time; but if left, they will of course lay eggs, and the resulting larvae will start operations at once.

label: text
text: An entomological friend told us a very amusing experience of his illustrating this fallacy. He gets

label: text
text: his friends to collect moths and butterflies for him, and on calling one day at the house of a fair collector, she showed him a very fine living specimen of the Emperor-moth (Saturala pavonia minor), which she had caught for him. Not knowing how to kill it, she had kept it alive for several days, and, moreover, out of the kindness of her gentle heart, she had fed it. On being asked what she had fed it on, she replied ingeniously, "Oh, I gave it a bit of old rag to eat!"

label: text
text: Some moths do not eat anything, as they have a sufficient store of nutrient to enable them to fulfil their mission in life, after which they die young. Others sip the nectar from flowers, and it is the flowers which open at night that are most strongly scented for the purpose of attracting the moths by their sense of smell, that of sight being useless in the dark.

Also white belongs to the moon in particular and thus is exceptionally fortunate to “moon folk,” another instance of the early worship of Isis, and how her influence has come down to us through so many other faiths. Rather curiously, white animals are considered unlucky. In many parts of England a white cat is called the sign of ill fortune, while in the Midlands they say you must be sure to spit if you meet a white horse face to face, spitting being a powerful spell to avert evil. And in Northamptonshire the unexpected sight of a white mouse is the sure foreruner of a death in the family.

label: text
text: us in old times, as to become a part of the name of various festal meetings, as Leet-ale, Lamb-ale, Bride-ale (bridal), and, as we see, Whitsun-ale. It was the custom of our ancestors to have parochial meetings every Whitsuntide, usually in some barn near the church, consisting of a kind of picnic, as each parishioner brought what victuals he could spare. The ale, which had been brewed pretty strong for the occasion was sold by the churchwardens, and from its profits a fund arose for the repair of the church.

At one of the London police-
courts the other day a gentleman
was charged with drunkenness.
What entitles his case to honour-
able mention is his defence. A
doctor went into the box and
swore that "his condition was due
to spastic paraplegia." Yet the
magistrate was not satisfied. He
replied, all too curtily, "What is
that?" Possibly he thought
there was some confusion: that
spastic paraplegia was a phrase
devised to test the power of
speech of one suspected of
inebriety, for which purpose,
indeed, it seems worthy of the
attention of the medical profession.
Possibly he suspected a
misunderstanding — for to the
mere layman it would seem that
spastic paraplegia ought to mean
some sort of drawn or contracted
paralysis. But it is ever rash to
assume that men of science use
their technical terms to mean
what the words ought to mean.
According to the testifying
doctor, spastic paraplegia really
means "acute nervous exhaustion." Then, said the disgusted
cadi, "Why not use plain English?" When the doctor explained
that it was "not the custom," the cadi exhorted him to change
that custom, complaining that "the medical profession has received sufficient hints from the
legal profession as to what is the proper thing to do and they will
not take notice." There speaks the bitterness of the man who has had to wrestle with experts in the witness-box. But we depreciate any attempt to make one profession the censor of another. "Such esoteric vocabularies are always being built up among people who have intercourse and interests a little apart from the rest of the world. Many families have their private slang. Each generation of undergraduates invents some of its own. Any popular game acquires, decade after decade, a mass of peculiar phrases devised by the players of the period. "W. G." knew not the googly, nor Arthur Shrewsbury the cow-shot. Some of these terms are needed to express new things, many of them are mere decorations of language. Even the most learned of the professions and the most austere of the sciences are not exempt from the common human instinct to be decorative in speech. It does not please the expert to call a common phenomenon by a name which common men never heard of. When he has discovered a new fact or invented a new theory he loves to give it a name worthy of his own ingenuity. In general he feels that his dignity is enhanced by talking in a jargon which nobody else uses, as the Meteorological Office derives an exquisite satisfaction from reporting the weather in terms of millibars. Let us not blame him. We encourage him continually. We like our experts to be incomprehensible. When we consult our specialist, we want him to talk in words we never heard before. If he used plain English he would be as disappointing as if he said there was nothing the matter with us. We know at the back of our minds that neither the cause nor the cure of anything is revealed by giving it a name derived more or less estimates from the Greek language.
